title: The path and its fruit
hookLine: the Sakya teaching that the path and the result are joined

lines: LAMDRE: THE PATH AND ITS FRUIT.
cards: An apple tree in a backyard, in early spring. No apples yet, only bare twigs and a few hard buds. Is the apple there?

In one sense, obviously not: there's nothing to pick. In another sense, it's already on its way, folded into the bud, waiting on sun and water and time. The tree isn't a different thing from the fruit.
It's the fruit, still happening. The Sakya school treasures a teaching built on a question close to that one: if awakening is the fruit, where is it while you're still walking the path?
Its name is Lamdre, the path and its fruit.

teach.b: First, the word. Lam is path. Dre is fruit, or result.

Lamdre is the path together with its result, and in Sakya it is a treasured body of teaching, passed down with great care, sometimes only to those who have asked for it and prepared. Second, where it came from.
The Sakya tradition traces Lamdre back to Virupa, an Indian master remembered in stories as a wild and powerful yogi.

teach.h: FROM VIRUPA TO THE KHON FAMILY.
teach.b: Tradition says his teaching came to Tibet and was kept by the Khon family, so the household that held the throne also held this teaching. Third, the idea itself.
On plenty of journeys, the road and the destination are separate: you suffer the highway to reach the beach.
Lamdre teaches that the qualities of awakening, clarity and openness, are already present in the mind as its nature, the way the apple is present in the bud.
Practice doesn't manufacture them from nothing; it uncovers and ripens what is there.

teach.h: THE RESULT IS ALREADY IN THE CAUSE.
teach.b: That's why Sakya teachers speak of the cause, the path and the result as joined, and why some speak of the round of suffering and nirvana as not finally two. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day.
If the fruit only exists at the end, today is just a toll you pay to get there.
If the path is already the fruit, today's patience is a piece of awakening, not a ticket to it. A small kind word isn't a down payment. It's the thing itself, in miniature.

how: In the Sakya school, Lamdre is taught by qualified teachers in formal transmissions, often over extended sessions, to students who request it and then practice its meditations.

o: a long road you finish before any reward comes
the path and its fruit, joined from the start
a Tibetan word for the harvest after a retreat

games.q: the path and its fruit: tap the pairs.
p: the Indian master it is traced to

s: Lamdre teaches that practice builds awakening out of nothing
it teaches that awakening's qualities are already present, and practice uncovers and ripens them.
the Sakya tradition traces Lamdre to the Indian master Virupa
he's remembered as a powerful yogi whose teaching came to the Khon family.
in Lamdre, the path is only a toll to pay before the result
it teaches that the path and the result are joined.

games.q: you're halfway through a long sit, restless, waiting for the good part. what would a Lamdre teacher point you toward?
o: push through: the reward comes at the end.
this restless breath is already part of the fruit.
games.why: Lamdre teaches the path and the result are joined, so the sit you're in is not a waiting room for awakening.

practice: Let the breath come and go, and notice the urge to get somewhere with this sit: calmer, clearer, done. Set the destination down; this breath isn't on the way to a good meditation, it is the meditation.
When the mind runs ahead, bring it back to the breath happening now, as if it were already the fruit you were waiting for.

wordCard.voice: Lamdre. The path and its fruit: the Sakya teaching that the result of practice is already present in the practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan: lam 'bras, path (lam) and fruit or result ('bras).

carryVoice: Your line: the path is the fruit. The dishes and the commute count too. I'll be here tomorrow.
